title: The Caricature and the Genome
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, the Neanderthals served as a convenient foil: brutish, slow and doomed, they flattered their successors by comparison. The sequencing of their DNA has unsettled that flattering story.

When researchers compared the first Neanderthal genome, sequenced in twenty ten, with the genomes of living people, they found that many of us carry fragments of it. Early estimates placed the share of Neanderthal ancestry in non-Africans at between one and four percent; a later study published in the journal Cell in twenty twenty refined the figure to about one point seven or one point eight percent for Europeans and Asians. The implication is unavoidable: the two populations met and had children, probably on more than one occasion.

The same study complicated the picture in a second way. Africans in the sample, long assumed to carry almost no Neanderthal DNA, were found to carry about seventeen million Neanderthal base pairs on average, roughly a third of the amount in Europeans and Asians. The authors suggested that gene flow had run in both directions, with some Neanderthal-like sequences travelling back to Africa with early modern humans.

Every such finding carries limits, and these deserve equal attention. The team sampled only a limited number of African populations, so the results may not generalise to everyone of African ancestry. Moreover, the Neanderthal genome used as a reference came from Siberia, and that population may not have been the one that actually interbred with the humans who left Africa.

Taken together, the findings replace a flattering caricature with something more interesting: a people who did not vanish without trace, but whose genetic traces persist in many of us. Whether that persistence reflects friendship, rivalry or something in between remains unknown, and an honest account must say so. Honest science rarely offers a finished story, but it offers a truthful one.
